newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi sugar refinery aims to start in two years.
newsitem.headline: Saudi sugar refinery aims to start in two years.

text.p: A Saudi Arabian agricultural company expects to start production at the kingdom's second sugar refinery in the next two years, its director general said.

Abdul Aziz al-Tilas of al-Jouf Agricultural Development Co (Jadco) said in a written reply to Reuters questions his company had recently received government approval for the 120,000 tonne annual refinery at Buseita al-Jouf in northern Saudi Arabia.
The refinery is expected to cost some 335 million riyals ($89 million).
The plant will refine locally-grown sugar beet. As well as producing sugar, 42,000 tonnes of molasses and 51,000 tonnes of animal feed would be produced annually, Tilas said.
"Our company has carried out experiments on sugar beet production and improvement in cooperation with German, Dutch and Egyptian companies for a few years," Tilas said.
Company officials said sugar beet production was still in the experimental phase and so far between three and five hectares of the crop had been cultivated.
A Jadco official said, "Our whole project area is almost 60,000 hectares."
"We will grow beet and there are another four big companies around us who can support us," he said.

Jouf, close to the border with Jordan, is one of the desert kingdom's cooler areas. It is about 500 km from the Red Sea. But annual rainfall in the area is only between 50 and 85 mm, with a maximum of around 100 mm in some years. The growing season is from September to April.
"But production is as high as it is in places like Germany, reaching a maximum of 80 tonnes per hectare, with up to 19 percent sugar. It is very promising," one official said.
Tilas said Jadco had started inviting tenders for the construction of the plant, which he said was expected to begin within a year.
The Saudi Industrial Development Fund will provide loans for half the cost of the plant. Another 25 percent will come from bank loans, and the rest will be provided by Jadco, he said.
Tilas said the refinery's output would be sold into the local market, where per capita sugar consumption among the kingdom's 18 million people is about 30 kg.

Total annual consumption in Saudi Arabia is around 550,000 tonnes, but is expanding amid population growth of three to four percent a year. Jadco will compete with the kingdom's only other refinery -- the United Sugar Co in Jeddah, which in February started commissioning its 500,000 tonne plant.
The start of production in Jeddah means that Saudi Arabia is fast becoming a predominantly raw sugar market.
The USC refinery is 51 percent owned by Savola -- Saudi Arabia's biggest food group, 15 percent by Britain's Tate and Lyle Plc and the rest by Saudi sugar trading firms.
